summary:
GeoSonora, created by the NEXUS team (Aranelys, Noel, Shantal, Robert, Miguelina, and Garian) for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, "The Earth Information Disc Machine," transforms NASA's open climate data into an inclusive, real-time auditory experience.

Satellite data is often presented in maps and charts that exclude people with visual impairments and make it difficult to perceive the speed of climate change. GeoSonora solves this problem with a website (https://earth-jukebox-nasa-2026.netlify.app) and an offline desktop app for Windows, offering two modes:

1. NASA Maps: Five official NASA SVS discs—Planetary Fever (#4882, 1880–2020), Global CO₂ Pulse (#5024, 2002–2022), Aerosol Symphony (#5552), Rising Oceans (#4853, 1992–2019), and Water and Soil Cycle (#4718, 2018–2019)—with year selector, automatic sweep, and manual sounding.

2. Tables/CSV: Allows you to paste tables or load official CSV files (such as GISTEMP) to listen to each record year by year.

Using React 19, TypeScript, Canvas 2D, Tone.js, and the Web Audio API, each magnitude is live-converted to Hertz frequencies over an 18-note pentatonic scale (130.8 to 1318.5 Hz), with a low-pass filter (600–3800 Hz) and West–East stereo panning. Features include Spanish voiceover (V), hide map (B), sound calibration, and full keyboard control.
details:
Technical Documentation - GeoSonora (NASA Space Apps 2026)

GeoSonora is a web platform and desktop application created by the five members of team NEXUS —Ara, Noel, Shantal, Robert, and Garian— for the Earth Information Jukebox challenge of the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge. Since NASA climate information is usually presented only in visual maps and numerical tables that exclude people with visual disabilities and make it difficult to perceive the speed of planetary changes, our solution converts that open science into an auditory, inclusive, and real-time experience.

Instead of using pre-recorded music, GeoSonora analyzes the pixels of five official NASA satellite records —global temperature, CO₂, aerosols, sea level, and water cycle— or processes public NASA tables and CSV files. Through Tone.js and the Web Audio API, each value is translated into frequencies in Hertz: low or negative readings sound in deep, soft, and slow tones, while recent spikes ascend to high-pitched, bright, and fast tones that convey urgency. With West-to-East stereo panning, a year selector, a mode to hide the map with the B key, keyboard control, and a Spanish voice narrator with the V key, anyone can intuitively and autonomously listen to Earth's climate history.

PROYECT DEMOSTRATION:

Online web application: https://earth-jukebox-nasa-2026.netlify.app ·

DEMO SLIDE:

https://canva.link/q2um44rmb72dido.

  1. Module Executive Summary (For Mentoring)

Our module programs the complete logical operation of GeoSonora in a simple and autonomous way: every fifty milliseconds it analyzes the actual color of the pixels on the active map on screen or reads each record of an imported time series, converting those scientific variations into live-generated sound. Each normalized magnitude is assigned to a consonant 18-note pentatonic scale between C3 and E6 (130.8 to 1318.5 Hz) along with a dynamic low-pass filter (600 to 3800 Hz) and three auditory calibration buttons per record so that anyone can immediately identify what each sound register represents.

The technical objective of the module is to independently solve the logical core of this Earth Jukebox, exclusively taking charge of extracting chromatic values from real NASA satellite visualizations or official CSV tables, transforming them into precise physical magnitudes, and synthesizing a musical and accessible response directly in the web browser or in the Windows desktop application, without relying on external servers or additional integrations.

2.Technical Description and Operating Logic

GeoSorona's logic operates through a continuous flow of inputs, processing, and outputs in two complementary modes: NASA Maps and Tables or CSV. In map mode, the system receives five scientific visualizations from NASA SVS, the active reading coordinate (either by automatic West-to-East sweep or by manual positioning with a mouse or keyboard arrow keys), temporal selection by years, volume, and accessibility commands. During processing, the visual module draws each frame onto a 960 by 540-pixel HTML5 Canvas and samples it on a hidden auxiliary canvas of 240 by 135 pixels; every fifty milliseconds it averages a three-by-three pixel neighborhood around the probe to avoid compression noise, converts the RGB color to HSL space, and translates it to the corresponding physical value according to the active record, assigning that normalized value to an eighteen-note pentatonic musical scale between C3 and E6 (130.8 to 1318.5 Hz) along with latitude, longitude, and approximate geographic region. In Tables and CSV mode, a syntactic parser interprets numerical lists pasted by the user or official NASA CSV files and plays back each record chronologically, varying the pitch in Hertz and the rhythm according to the magnitude of the data. As output, the audio engine built with Tone.js over Web Audio API synthesizes the note live using a polyphonic triangle-wave synthesizer connected to a dynamic low-pass filter (600 to 3800 Hz), a geographic stereo panner, soft reverb, and an on-screen oscilloscope, while the interface allows activating spoken reading in Spanish via Web Speech API.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"" ]

To build the platform, React 19 with TypeScript, Vite, and Tailwind CSS were used for the modular interface, HTML5 Canvas 2D for direct pixel reading, Tone.js for real-time sound synthesis, Web Speech API for accessible narration, and Electron to generate the Windows desktop application. Within team NEXUS, the five members collaborated in a coordinated manner: Aranelys led the project's introduction and closing; Robert framed the problem statement and structured the solution and importance of translating scientific data into auditory frequencies; Noel defined the general objective and the accessibility-oriented experience; Shantal took charge of the technical and functional development of the platform; and Garian compiled the datasets and official NASA sources that feed the application.

3. Resources and Data Sources Used

To feed the five records of the NASA Maps mode, the software uses official scientific visualizations from the NASA Scientific Visualization Studio (SVS) integrated locally in WebM and PNG format within the project's public folder, allowing pixels to be analyzed without CORS restrictions and guaranteeing offline operation in the desktop application. The first record, Planetary Fever (https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/4882/), uses the NASA SVS #4882 resource from NASA GISS Surface Temperature (GISTEMP) with global thermal anomalies from -2.0 to +2.0 degrees Celsius between 1880 and 2020; the second, Global CO₂ Pulse (https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/5024/), uses NASA SVS #5024 from the AIRS instrument aboard the Aqua satellite with concentrations from 370 to 425+ ppm between 2002 and 2022; the third, Aerosol Symphony (https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/5552/), processes the global panorama NASA SVS #5552 from NASA GMAO's GEOS-FP model measuring the AOD index of sea salt, Saharan dust, wildfire smoke, and sulfates; the fourth, Rising Oceans (https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/4853/), takes NASA SVS #4853 from the TOPEX/Poseidon and Jason-1/2/3 altimetry missions in a range of -100 to +100 millimeters between 1992 and 2019; and the fifth, Water and Soil Cycle (https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/4718/), incorporates NASA SVS #4718 from the SMAP and GPM IMERG missions (2018–2019), decoding its layers of liquid precipitation (0 to 0.001 kg/m²/s), snow depth (0.25 to 1.5 meters), surface soil moisture (0 to 1 wetness), snow, and ocean.0

Complementarily, the Tables / CSV mode links directly to the public records of NASA GISS Surface Temperature Analysis (https://data.giss.nasa.gov/gistemp/) and allows pasting web tables or loading official CSV files downloaded from NASA portals, automatically identifying standard year and average value columns such as Year, J-D, Glob, or Mean. Additionally, it includes three historical demonstration series based on global GISTEMP anomalies (2010–2023 and 1880–2023 in degrees Celsius) and carbon dioxide measurements (2014–2023 in ppm), backed by the outreach framework of the NASA Earth Information Center portal (https://earth.gov).

Space Agency Partner Data and Other References: No datasets from external partner space agencies were used; all scientific information, satellite visualizations, and numerical series come exclusively from official open NASA sources. As technical references and open-source tools employed in the implementation, Tone.js (https://tonejs.github.io) was used for real-time musical synthesis and filters; the Web Audio API and Web Speech API web standards (MDN / W3C documentation) for stereo panning, dynamic filtering, and Spanish voice narration; React (https://react.dev), TypeScript, Vite (https://vite.dev), Tailwind CSS, and Lucide React for the modular interface; and Electron (https://www.electronjs.org) for the offline desktop application on Windows.

4. Code Deliverables and Prototype Testing

The project is delivered in three functional formats built from a single modular codebase in TypeScript and React 19: the source code structured with the official NASA SVS multimedia files in the public folder (public/nasa/), the sound synthesis modules (src/audio/), scientific decoding and CSV analysis (src/utils/), record catalog (src/data/), and user interface (src/components/), available at (GitHub - garianminaya-creator/earth-jukebox-nasa-2026); the web application published and publicly accessible at https://earth-jukebox-nasa-2026.netlify.app via configuration in netlify.toml; and the standalone desktop application for Windows packaged with Electron (electron/main.cjs), distributed both as a direct executable (GeoSonoe.exe) and as a compressed portable package (GeoSo-1.0.0-win.zip) with an internal server on 127.0.0.1 and range-streaming support to operate offline. Likewise, the slide demonstration of the prototype's operation is available at https://canva.link/q2um44rmb72dido.

To validate the prototype, the production build (tsc -b and vite build), generation of desktop binaries, and verification of public HTTP 200 access on the Netlify link were completed without errors, in addition to confirming in direct execution that the Windows executable starts its processes and loads Tone.js without console errors. In interactive browser tests, the operation of all five NASA SVS records was verified —including the multi-layer legend of the Water and Soil Cycle record (#4718)—, the automatic West-to-East sweep synchronized with notes and stereo panning, the manual probe with mouse and keyboard arrows, chronological scrolling by years in the videos, loading and sequential playback in Hertz within the Tables / CSV mode (reaching 1319 Hz at E6 for the +1.17 °C record of 2023), auditory calibration of three references per record, visual hiding with the B key, and the Spanish voice narrator with the V key.

(TOPEX/Poseidon & Jason-1/2/3, 1992–2019): Global video used in the "Océanos en Ascenso" disc to turn sea level anomalies (-100 to 100 mm) into sound.
